title: Extremal size of sunflower-free set families
formal: For each fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), determine, up to constant factors as \(k\to \infty , S_{r}(k)\): the largest number of distinct k-element sets in a family containing no r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, where the finite ground set is unrestricted.
definitions: The r members in a sunflower must be distinct. Their common pairwise intersection is the core, and deleting it leaves pairwise disjoint petals. For each integer \(k\ge 1\), take the maximum cardinality over all sunflower-free families on arbitrary finite universes. The classical sunflower bound makes these cardinalities bounded by an integer depending only on k,r, so the maximum exists despite the unrestricted universe. No algorithm or encoding bound is imposed. The parameter r is fixed before k grows; asymptotic constants may depend on r.

context_blocks.text: The target is the extremal function itself. The sunflower conjecture states that \(S_{r}(k)\) has at most exponential growth in k for each fixed r, a weaker qualitative question than matching its full asymptotic order.
Sunflowers capture a simple repeated pattern inside a large family of small sets. Bounds on their forced occurrence are basic tools in circuit complexity, pseudorandomness and kernelization.

The breakthrough bound of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang replaces a much larger dependence by roughly \((\log  k)^{O(k)}\) for fixed r. The conjecture asks for a constant base to the k-th power. This is admitted as a computationally motivated exception to the exclusion of general combinatorics, not to fill a combinatorics category.

why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
answer_criterion: Give functions \(f_{r}(k)\) and, for every fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), constants \(0<c_{r}\le C_{r}<\infty\) with \(c_{r} f_{r}(k)\le S_{r}(k)\le C_{r} f_{r}(k)\) for every \(k\ge 1\), absorbing finitely many small k into the constants if needed. Prove both a universal upper bound and existence of matching sunflower-free families in Lean. An exponential upper bound by itself does not determine the growth within constant factors.

sentences: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets with one common pairwise intersection.
For fixed r, the target is the maximum size of a family of k-element sets containing no r-member sunflower.
Determine its growth as k increases within constant factors that may depend on r.
The ground set is any finite universe and the question imposes no algorithmic restrictions.
The sunflower conjecture predicts at most exponential growth, a weaker claim than determining the full extremal order.
